title: Chapter 2 — That Democracy Renders The Habitual Intercourse Of The Americans Simple And Easy
paragraphs: Democracy does not bind men strongly to one another, but it places their habitual interactions on an easier footing. If two Englishmen happen to meet at the Antipodes, surrounded by strangers whose language and manners are almost unknown to them, they will first stare at each other with great curiosity and a kind of secret uneasiness; they will then turn away, or, if one addresses the other, they will take care to converse only with a constrained and absent air on very unimportant subjects. Yet there is no enmity between these men; they have never seen each other before, and each believes the other to be a respectable person. Why then do they stand so cautiously apart? We must go back to England to learn the reason.

When birth alone, independent of wealth, classes men in society, everyone knows exactly where he stands on the social scale; he does not seek to rise, and he does not fear to fall. In a community so organized, men of different castes communicate very little with each other; but if chance brings them together, they are ready to converse without hoping or fearing to lose their own position. Their intercourse is not on a footing of equality, but it is not constrained. When an aristocracy of money succeeds an aristocracy of birth, the case is altered. The privileges of some are still extremely great, but the possibility of acquiring those privileges is open to all; from which it follows that those who possess them are constantly haunted by the fear of losing them, or of other men sharing them. Those who do not yet enjoy them long to possess them at any cost, or at least to appear to possess them — which is not impossible. Since the social importance of men is no longer ostensibly and permanently fixed by blood, and is infinitely varied by wealth, ranks still exist, but it is not easy to distinguish at a glance who belongs to which. Secret hostilities then arise in the community: one set of men strive by countless artifices to penetrate, or appear to penetrate, among those above them; another set are constantly on guard against these usurpers of their rights; or rather the same individual does both at once, and while he tries to raise himself into a higher circle, he is always on the defensive against the intrusion of those below him.

Such is the condition of England at the present time; and I am of the opinion that the peculiarity mentioned above is principally attributable to this cause. Since aristocratic pride is still extremely strong among the English, and since the limits of aristocracy are ill-defined, everyone lives in constant fear of someone taking advantage of his familiarity. Unable to judge at once the social position of those he meets, an Englishman prudently avoids all contact with them. Men are afraid that some slight service rendered may draw them into an unsuitable acquaintance; they dread civilities, and they avoid a stranger's obtrusive gratitude as much as his hatred. Many people attribute these singular anti-social tendencies, and the reserved and taciturn bearing of the English, to purely physical causes. I may admit that there is something of this in their race, but much more of it is attributable to their social condition, as is proved by the contrast of the Americans.

In America, where the privileges of birth never existed, and where wealth confers no special rights on those who possess it, men who do not know each other are very willing to frequent the same places, and find neither peril nor advantage in the free exchange of their thoughts. If they meet by chance, they neither seek nor avoid interaction; their manner is therefore natural, frank, and open. It is easy to see that they hardly expect or apprehend anything from each other, and that they do not care either to display or to conceal their position in the world. If their demeanor is often cold and serious, it is never haughty or constrained; and if they do not converse, it is because they are not in the mood to talk, not because they think it in their interest to be silent. In a foreign country, two Americans are instantly friends, simply because they are Americans. They are repelled by no prejudice; they are drawn together by their common country. For two Englishmen, shared blood is not enough; they must be brought together by shared rank. The Americans notice this unsociable mood of the English as much as the French do, and they are no less astonished by it. Yet the Americans are connected with England by their origin, their religion, their language, and in part by their manners; they differ only in their social condition. It may therefore be inferred that the reserve of the English proceeds from the constitution of their country much more than from that of its inhabitants.
